source: Jia et al. (2025) PISA: Piaget-inspired schema memory, arXiv 2510.15966
finding: PISA has one ablation, on AggQA only. It removes the schema-driven initialisation (PISA-I) or makes retrieval blind to the memory hierarchy (PISA-R). It does not ablate the update, evolution or creation steps (assimilation vs accommodation).
numbers: PISA-I Medical overall acc 69.39 vs full 83.67 (-14.28). PISA-R Financial overall acc 51.77 vs full 69.41 (-17.64); hard tasks 78.57 to 50.00.
limits: No LOCOMO ablation. The core schema-revision mechanism stays untested.
agent_relevance: Structure and schema-guided retrieval help; the Piagetian revision step itself is not shown to matter. Gap 5 stays open for PISA.

source: Jia et al. (2025) PISA, Table 1 LOCOMO (updated loose judge)
finding: On LOCOMO PISA beats other memory systems at far fewer tokens than full context, and with the loose judge matches full context on average.
numbers: Average LLM-judge acc: PISA 74.80 (2.1k tokens/query), FullContext 74.02 (21.09k), LangMem 71.97 (0.76k), MemoryOS 64.33 (7.44k), Mem0 64.21 (6.34k), AMem 61.53 (3.11k). Adversarial: PISA 76.24 vs full context 54.01.
limits: Judge prompt changed from the earlier version, so older K19 figures (63.58 vs 55.51 vs 68.47) are not comparable. No Piaget-specific ablation.
agent_relevance: Cheap structured memory can match long context; the Piaget label adds nothing proven.

finding: CAM ablates two Piaget-named parts. Removing structured hierarchy hurts most; removing flexible assimilation (ego-centric disentangling) hurts less; both always below full CAM. Dynamic accommodation is evaluated in an online batch test, not ablated.
numbers: Full CAM ACC-L: NovelQA 52.3, QMSum 57.6, ODSum-S 54.6. w/o Hierarchy 46.7, 46.6, 49.3. w/o Flexibility 50.3, 51.5, 51.2. Best baseline RAPTOR NovelQA 47.8, QMSum 50.7.
limits: Table header had mismatched columns in the HTML; column mapping inferred. The parts are clustering and label propagation with Piagetian names.
agent_relevance: Gains come from hierarchy and propagation, which are ordinary engineering parts. Partly closes gap 5 for assimilation.

source: SCG-Mem: To Know is to Construct, schema-constrained generation for agent memory, arXiv 2604.20117
finding: This paper ablates assimilation (grounding to existing schema nodes), keeping accommodation only. Removing it cuts every LoCoMo category by 20-35 percent. Accommodation alone is never tested.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B: full multi-hop F1 28.49 vs 18.74 without (-34.2%); temporal 42.29 vs 33.79; single-hop 42.51 vs 33.73; adversarial 52.63 vs 34.33 (-34.8%). Avg F1 41.48 vs A-MEM 21.33.
limits: One small model, one ablation arm. Models 1B-3B only.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that schema-grounded revision (assimilate first, accommodate on failure) beats free-form memory writes, in small models. Gap 5 mostly closed for assimilation.

source: Nickel et al. (2026) Understanding artificial theory of mind: perturbed tasks and reasoning in LLMs, arXiv 2602.22072
finding: False-belief tasks with 10 perturbation types (1,088 questions, 6 open chat models). CoT helps a lot on clean items but little under perturbation, and hurts on some perturbations. The paper excludes RL-trained reasoning models, so it does not answer the reasoning-model part of gap 8.
numbers: Avg across models: clean V-P 67.2 to CoT 89.6 (+22.4); perturbed V-P 49.9 to CoT 53.8 (+3.9). Biggest CoT gain Untrustworthy Testimony +25.0; drops Conclusion from Sentiment -12.1, Automatic Change Knowledge -12.1. Only Llama-3-70B and DBRX reach limited robustness. Faithfulness phi 0.306-0.584.
limits: Models are 2023-24 vintage; no o1/R1 style models.
agent_relevance: Prompt framing changes false-belief accuracy by tens of points. A scaffold must be tested on perturbed items, not clean classics.

source: Powell, Hobbs, Bardis, Carey, Saxe (2018) Replications of implicit theory of mind tasks with varying representational demands, Cognitive Development
finding: Two violation-of-expectation tasks failed to show that 18-month-olds expect an agent to act on a false belief. Looking times did not differ between expected and unexpected reaches. Interactive tasks partly replicated.
numbers: Task 2: expected M=21.0 s vs unexpected 18.3 s, no effect (P>0.1); first trial 20.7 vs 18.8 s, t(41)=0.76. Task 3: 18.1 vs 16.5 s (P>0.3); first trial 17.6 vs 17.4 s, t(77)=0.09. One 2-year-old interactive task fully replicated.
quote: Looking times were consistent with infants having no clear prediction about the agent's actions.
limits: About false-belief VoE, not object permanence. Does not test the drawbridge.
agent_relevance: Early-competence claims from looking time are weak; do not use infant VoE as a design anchor.

source: Wenzel, Dorrenberg, Proft, Liszkowski, Rakoczy (2020) Actions do not speak louder than words in an interactive false belief task, Royal Society Open Science
finding: Replication of an interactive false-belief task failed. The original did not replicate in 17-month-olds or 3-year-olds. The paper notes VoE conceptual replications have given very mixed results but gives no VoE numbers.
numbers: Original N=60 17-month-olds. Study 1: 48 17-month-olds and 48 3-year-olds, chance. Study 2a N=40, 2b N=36 (24 months): no belief tracking. Study 3a N=24 (3;6-4;6). 3b N=48 adults.
agent_relevance: Same lesson: early-ability findings often vanish under tighter tests.

source: Bogartz, Shinskey, Schilling (2000) Object permanence in 5.5-month-old infants? Infancy 1(4)
finding: Event-set designs on Baillargeon's rotating-screen task. Looking times follow novelty and familiarity relative to habituation, not possible vs impossible. Fewer familiarisation trials gave preference for the familiar event.
numbers: Exp 1: 36 infants (5m3d to 6m6d), 3 habituation groups, mean trials to criterion 7.50, 6.75, 7.58 (F(2,33)=.80). Exp 2: 52 infants familiarised on 3 or 7 trials. Model R2=.624, F(39,105)=12.18; possibility parameter not significant (F(1,104)=.0097, p=.92).
quote: Infants did not use the possibility or impossibility of events.
limits: Small samples. No multi-lab replication of either side found. Knowledge-account researchers dispute the model.
agent_relevance: Looking-time contrasts depend on design details; treat as unsettled. Gap 7 stays open.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning, ICLR; arXiv 2205.10625
finding: Closest tested analogue of a stage-ordered scaffold: solve easier sub-problems first and feed answers forward. It beats chain-of-thought on length generalisation, but on GSM8K the gain is small and grows with step count.
numbers: SCAN length split (code-davinci-002): standard 16.7, CoT 16.2, least-to-most 99.7. GSM8K 62.39 vs CoT 60.87 (4-step 59.73 vs 59.39; 5-step 45.23 vs 39.07). DROP non-football 82.45 vs 74.77; football 73.42 vs 59.56.
limits: 2022 model, few-shot, not equal-token controlled (two prompt stages). Not a Piaget study.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: decomposition-first beats plain CoT where the problem is longer than the demos; edge is small on GSM8K. No equal-token test on a modern reasoning model found.

finding: Blank-image and no-image text controls show a strong bias to answer Conserve without visual content. So the 85.7 percent figure is mostly a prior, and real images lower it.
numbers: Empty image: 85.7% stay Conserve; 71.5% of True-More and 75.4% of True-Less items flipped to Conserve. Text only: 73.7%, 69.1%, 68.2%. With real visuals conservation about 60%. Adding an I-dont-know option (10 models): bias persisted, r=0.591 blank, 0.362 text, p<0.0001.
quote: visual content actively interferes with the textual prior
limits: 62 VLMs, 7-frame condition. No shuffled-image control. Authors still read the deficit as visual transformation reasoning, which the controls do not prove.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: answer is mostly response bias; text-only agents show it too (73.7%). Test with balanced conserve and non-conserve items.

source: Relational complexity bottleneck in LLMs (REL), arXiv 2604.12176, controlled biology task B1
finding: With other parameters fixed (50 leaves, sequence length 1000, motif length 50), relational complexity alone explains the largest share of variance in the biology task. Gap 4 closed in part.
numbers: REL-B1 accuracy falls from 35% at 4 homoplastic taxa to 1% at 25. RC explains 24% (Claude Opus 4.5), 32% (Gemini 3 Pro), 44% (GPT-5.2) of explainable variance; next factor 6-17%.
limits: Three frontier models; averages only. In chemistry C1 vs C2 (both RC=2) operand complexity matters too.
agent_relevance: RC is a real predictor when controlled; keep it as a task-design variable, not the only one.

source: REL chemistry and intervention results, arXiv 2604.12176
finding: Entity count barely matters at fixed RC; operand complexity matters a lot. More test-time compute did nothing; one-shot examples helped a little; an RDKit tool did not help the highest-RC task.
numbers: C1 65.7% (56.0 at 5 molecules to 71.0 at 50); C2 38.1% (flat about 39.2 +/- 2.6); C3 26.0%. Extra compute about +0.4 pts. One-shot: C1 77.0 (+6.6), C2 43.3 (+3.4), C3 32.7 (+6.0). RDKit C3 recall 0.094.
agent_relevance: Capacity limits are not fixed by tokens or tools; shrink the binding load per step instead.

source: Strong Memory, Weak Control, arXiv 2504.02789v2, reasoning intervention
finding: Reasoning fixes flanker interference but not working-memory span or rule switching. It spends thousands of tokens on a task humans do in 300-500 ms.
numbers: Flanker incongruent: Llama-3.1-8B 0.471 to 0.910; Qwen2-32B 0.638 to 0.985. WCST: instruction-tuned 0.29-0.53 vs about 0.77 healthy adults; reasoning models with strategy hints did not beat non-reasoning; traces often unfinished at 30,000 tokens. No n-back test with reasoning.
quote: generate thousands of tokens to solve a task humans complete in 300-500ms
limits: No exact token counts per task and no WCST numbers for reasoning models in the text I got.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: an explicit stepwise trace fixes interference; rule switching needs an external state (a rule tracker), not more thinking.

source: Samuel and Bryant (1984) Asking only one question in the conservation experiment, J Child Psychol Psychiatry 25(2)
finding: Abstract confirms: Rose and Blank showed 6-year-olds do much better when asked once after the transformation; this experiment extends it to mass and volume and ages 5-8.
numbers: Abstract gives no counts. Secondary summaries (not opened) give 252 children, 4 age groups, 3 conditions (standard, one-question, fixed-array), fewer errors in one-question condition, number easiest. Exact means still not obtained.
quote: this important result applies as well to other materials (mass and volume) and to a wide age range (5-8 yr)
agent_relevance: Question repetition changes answers; avoid asking the same check twice in a loop.

source: Borke (1975) Piaget's mountains revisited, Developmental Psychology 11
finding: Not opened. Only the index record and a study-guide snippet. Child-friendly farm scene with Grover; 3-year-olds correct 79 percent, 4-year-olds 93 percent per the snippet.
numbers: 79% (age 3) and 93% (age 4), from a secondary study guide, not verified.
limits: Unverified. Piaget and Inhelder 1956 numbers were not found either.
agent_relevance: Treat 79/93 as unconfirmed; task familiarity moves success years earlier.

source: Neo-Piagetian M-capacity measurement (1996, Intelligence) and a linearity test with the Figural Intersections Test, N=215, ages 5-12
finding: Not opened. Snippet says FIT-based estimates sat above predicted scale values and the study only partly supported Pascual-Leone's linear M growth. Pascual-Leone's own age tables were not obtained.
limits: Snippet only; could not tell which paper the 215 study was.
agent_relevance: Capacity ladders are approximate; keep them out of the schema.

source: Sirois and Jackson drawbridge replication (as summarised in search snippets)
finding: Snippet only: the original looking effect replicated, but infants also looked longer at 180-degree events overall, so it does not warrant an object-permanence reading.
Large multi-lab replication of Hamlin 2007 reportedly did not reproduce the preference. Nearest multi-lab infant result found. No multi-lab drawbridge or object-permanence study found.
numbers: Coverage reports 56 percent reach for one character, indistinguishable from chance; not verified.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no direct multi-lab test of object permanence found.
